prompt: The short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve describes the relationship between

options.label: A
options.text: the interest rate and the quantity of investment goods supplied by firms.

options.label: B
options.text: the price level and the quantity of goods and services supplied in an economy.

options.label: C
options.text: the price level and the quantity of goods and services demanded by households and firms.

options.label: D
options.text: the wage rate and the number of workers willing to supply their labor.

options.label: E
options.text: nominal GDP and the overall level of employment in the economy.

explanation: The SRAS curve shows the relationship between the overall price level (vertical axis) and the total quantity of real GDP supplied by all producers in the economy (horizontal axis). It is a macroeconomic, economy-wide relationship - not a single market supply curve.

prompt: On an SRAS curve graph, the axes are correctly labeled as

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: E

explanation: The SRAS graph uses Price Level on the vertical axis and Real GDP on the horizontal axis. This is the same axis labeling as the AD curve, and both together form the AD-AS model; using "Price" and "Quantity" (microeconomic labels) would be incorrect.

prompt: The SRAS curve is upward-sloping because

options.label: A
options.text: higher wages in the short run make workers willing to supply more labor.

options.label: B
options.text: higher price levels attract more foreign investment, increasing domestic production.

options.label: C
options.text: wages and input prices are sticky in the short run — they do not immediately rise with the price level — so higher output prices raise firm profit margins, inducing more production.

options.label: D
options.text: government spending automatically increases when the price level rises.

options.label: E
options.text: firms always increase output when the price level rises because demand always rises with prices.

explanation: The SRAS curve slopes upward because wages and input prices are sticky (slow to adjust) in the short run. When the overall price level rises while input costs remain temporarily fixed, firms' profit margins widen; this makes additional production more profitable, so firms increase the quantity supplied; the stickiness of wages and prices is the key mechanism.

prompt: In the context of the SRAS curve, "sticky wages" means

options.label: A
options.text: wages rise instantly and fully in response to any increase in the price level.

options.label: B
options.text: wages are fixed by the government and cannot change under any circumstances.

options.label: C
options.text: nominal wages are slow to adjust in the short run — they do not immediately increase when the price level rises — because of contracts, social norms, and information lags.

options.label: D
options.text: wages are always higher than the price level in the short run.

options.label: E
options.text: real wages remain constant even when nominal wages change.

explanation: MOD-2.E.1: Sticky wages are wages that do not adjust immediately to changes in the price level in the short run. Workers may have multi-year contracts, employers may be reluctant to cut wages due to morale effects, or workers and firms may not yet realize that the price level has changed; this stickiness means that when output prices rise, input costs (wages) lag behind, widening profit margins and inducing more production.

prompt: The short run, in the context of the SRAS curve, is best defined as the period in which

options.label: A
options.text: real GDP is always equal to potential GDP and all resources are fully employed.

options.label: B
options.text: all prices and wages are perfectly flexible and adjust immediately to equilibrium.

options.label: C
options.text: some input prices — particularly wages — are fixed or slow to adjust, so changes in the price level affect profit margins and the quantity firms choose to supply.

options.label: D
options.text: the government has not yet implemented fiscal policy in response to economic conditions.

options.label: E
options.text: only the government sector's prices are flexible; all private sector prices are fixed.

explanation: The short run is defined as the period in which some input prices - especially nominal wages - are fixed or sticky. Because input costs do not immediately adjust, changes in the overall price level create temporary changes in profit margins, which affect the quantity of real GDP supplied; this is in contrast to the long run, where all wages and prices are fully flexible.

prompt: Which of the following correctly states the direction of the SRAS curve's slope?

options.label: A
options.text: Downward-sloping — as the price level rises, the quantity of real GDP supplied falls.

options.label: B
options.text: Perfectly horizontal — the price level does not affect the quantity supplied in the short run.

options.label: C
options.text: Perfectly vertical — the quantity supplied is fixed regardless of the price level in the short run.

options.label: D
options.text: Upward-sloping — as the price level rises, the quantity of real GDP supplied increases, because sticky wages and input prices make higher output prices profitable for firms.

options.label: E
options.text: U-shaped — the SRAS first falls then rises as the price level increases.

explanation: The SRAS curve is upward-sloping (positive slope). A higher price level - with wages and input costs temporarily fixed - increases firm profit margins, motivating firms to expand output; A lower price level - with input costs sticky - compresses margins, causing firms to reduce output; the upward slope reflects this sticky-cost mechanism.

prompt: A rightward shift of the SRAS curve indicates that

options.label: A
options.text: the price level has risen, causing firms to supply more at any given output level.

options.label: B

options.label: E

explanation: A rightward shift of the SRAS curve means producers are willing and able to supply more real GDP at every given price level - typically because production costs have fallen (e.g., lower wages, cheaper raw materials, improved productivity). The entire curve moves right, reflecting an increase in short-run aggregate supply.

prompt: A leftward shift of the SRAS curve indicates that

The entire curve moves left, reflecting a decrease in short-run aggregate supply.

prompt: According to MOD-2.C.3, which of the following causes the SRAS curve to shift?

options.label: A
options.text: A change in the price level.

options.label: B
options.text: A change in consumer spending on final goods and services.

explanation: The CED explicitly states: "Any factor that causes production costs to change, such as a change in inflationary expectations, will cause the SRAS curve to shift." Key cost-shifting factors include: wages/input prices, raw material prices (especially oil), inflationary expectations, productivity, business taxes, and government regulations. A price level change causes movement ALONG the curve, not a shift.

prompt: Economy Alpha has sticky wages. The price level rises from PL₁ to PL₂ (with wages unchanged). Trace the complete chain of reasoning for why the quantity of real GDP supplied increases.

options.text: Higher PL → output prices rise → wages and input costs remain sticky (unchanged) → firm profit margins widen (revenue per unit up, cost per unit unchanged) → firms increase production → economy moves from Y₁ to Y₂ along the SRAS curve.

prompt: Using MOD-2.D.1, trace the complete chain from a rise in the price level (movement up the SRAS curve) to the effect on unemployment. Assume the labor force is held constant.

prompt: A student draws an SRAS curve that is perfectly horizontal. Another draws one that is perfectly vertical. Which evaluation is correct?

prompt: Explain why the "sticky wages" explanation for the upward-sloping SRAS assumes that it is specifically NOMINAL wages (not real wages) that are sticky in the short run.

options.label: B
options.text: Nominal wages are what workers and employers negotiate in contracts — they are the dollar amounts written in wage agreements. When the price level rises, real wages (nominal wages adjusted for inflation) actually FALL in the short run because nominal wages are sticky. This falling real wage is what allows firms to profitably expand production.

options.label: C

Lower real wages mean labor is effectively cheaper for firms per unit of output → firms expand hiring and production; this is the mechanism: sticky nominal wages → falling real wages when PL rises → more production → upward-sloping SRAS.

prompt: Which of the following correctly explains why the SRAS curve shifts left when workers expect higher inflation, even BEFORE actual inflation occurs?

prompt: Explain what "sticky prices" (as opposed to "sticky wages") contribute to the upward slope of the SRAS curve.

options.label: B

prompt: A student argues: "If the SRAS slopes upward and the AD slopes downward, they must always intersect at potential GDP, because that's where supply equals demand." Evaluate this claim using only SRAS concepts from Topic 3.3.

options.label: A
options.text: Correct — the intersection of SRAS and AD always equals potential GDP by definition.

options.label: B
options.text: Incorrect — the SRAS slopes upward and can intersect the AD curve at any level of real GDP: above, below, or equal to potential GDP. The SRAS curve captures the short-run supply relationship between price level and output — it does not guarantee that the intersection occurs at potential GDP. Potential GDP is a separate concept (related to LRAS), and the short-run equilibrium can deviate from it.

options.label: C
options.text: Correct — because in the short run, all resources are fully employed.

options.label: D
options.text: Incorrect — SRAS and AD never intersect because they represent different sides of the market.

options.label: E
options.text: Correct — the SRAS always adjusts to intersect AD at potential GDP in the short run.

explanation: The SRAS describes the relationship between the price level and quantity supplied - it does not constrain where equilibrium occurs relative to potential GDP. The SRAS can intersect AD at output levels below potential (recessionary gap), at potential, or above potential (inflationary gap); the short-run equilibrium is wherever SRAS and AD intersect, which may or may not be at potential GDP.

prompt: Country Epsilon has wages set by one-year contracts. For the first six months after contracts are signed, wages are fully sticky. options.label: A
options.text: Second six months — more adjustable wages make supply more responsive.

options.label: B
options.text: First six months — perfectly sticky wages create the maximum profit-margin effect for a given PL change, producing the largest output response (flatter SRAS, more elastic supply). But wait — flatter means MORE elastic, so the SRAS is less steep in the first six months.

options.label: C
options.text: First six months — with fully sticky wages, a rise in the price level creates a maximum gap between output prices and fixed input costs. This produces the largest supply response per unit of PL change, meaning the SRAS is relatively flat (elastic). In the second six months, partial wage adjustability reduces the profit-margin effect → smaller supply response → SRAS is more steeply sloped (less elastic).

options.label: D

options.label: E

explanation: SRAS slope reflects the degree of wage stickiness; in the first six months - wages perfectly sticky → any PL rise creates a full profit-margin effect → large output response → relatively flat (elastic) SRAS. In the second six months - wages partially adjustable → PL rise partially offset by rising wages → smaller profit-margin effect → smaller output response → steeper (less elastic) SRAS; greater wage stickiness → flatter SRAS; less stickiness → steeper SRAS.

prompt: An economy's SRAS curve is given. A cost-push supply shock (rising oil prices) shifts SRAS left at the same time that a fall in aggregate demand (negative demand shock) also occurs. Which of the following correctly describes the effect on the price level and real GDP?

prompt: A government subsidizes the production of renewable energy, significantly reducing energy costs for all domestic firms. Using SRAS analysis, describe the effect on the SRAS curve and explain whether this is a shift or a movement.

prompt: Economy Theta: The SRAS curve slopes upward. A student claims: "The SRAS slopes up because producers want to earn higher profits — they always supply more when prices are higher, just like individual firms do." Evaluate whether the macroeconomic sticky-wage explanation is consistent with this student's intuition, and what nuance is missing.

options.label: B
options.text: The student's claim is partially correct as an intuition but misses the critical nuance: the SRAS slopes upward not simply because higher prices are attractive to producers, but specifically because input costs (wages) are sticky in the short run. If wages rose proportionally with output prices, profit margins would not widen and there would be no incentive to produce more. The upward slope depends on the lag between output prices and input costs.

options.label: C

options.label: D

If wages rose perfectly with prices, real wages and profit margins would be unchanged, giving no incentive to expand output; the key is the STICKINESS of input costs relative to output prices - this creates the profit-margin effect that drives the positive slope.

prompt: Country Sigma has an upward-sloping SRAS curve. A student argues that if wages were completely and instantaneously flexible (adjusted perfectly to every price level change), the SRAS curve would become perfectly horizontal. Output remains at its natural (potential) level regardless of the price level — a VERTICAL supply curve. This is the LRAS, not an intermediate horizontal SRAS.

The upward-sloping SRAS exists specifically because of IMPERFECT (sticky) wage adjustment; perfect flexibility → vertical, not horizontal.

prompt: A student encounters this argument: "Since the SRAS is upward-sloping and the short-run trade-off (from MOD-2.D.1) means lower unemployment is associated with higher price levels, a policymaker who wants low unemployment should just let the price level rise indefinitely." Evaluate this policy argument using only 3.3 SRAS concepts.

options.label: A
options.text: Correct — permanently higher price levels always maintain lower unemployment.

options.label: B
options.text: Incorrect — the trade-off is TEMPORARY. Higher price levels reduce unemployment only because wages are sticky in the short run. As wages adjust upward (in the long run, or as contracts expire), the profit-margin advantage disappears, real wages restore, and unemployment returns to its natural rate. Permanently rising price levels (continuous inflation) would require continuously accelerating inflation to sustain the profit-margin effect — an unsustainable strategy. The short-run trade-off is not a permanent policy tool.

options.label: C
options.text: Correct — higher price levels always keep unemployment below the natural rate.

options.label: D
options.text: Incorrect — higher price levels always RAISE unemployment by discouraging production.

options.label: E
options.text: Correct — policymakers should target the highest sustainable price level to minimize unemployment.

explanation: MOD-2.E.1: The short-run trade-off (higher PL → lower unemployment) is specifically SHORT-RUN; it exists because wages are sticky. As wages adjust upward (MOD-2.E.1 - long-run flexibility), the profit-margin advantage that reduced unemployment disappears; output returns to potential and unemployment to the natural rate. To sustain lower unemployment through higher prices, the price level would need to keep rising faster than wages continuously - requiring ever-accelerating inflation; the trade-off is a short-run phenomenon, not a sustainable long-run policy tool.

prompt: An economy has perfectly competitive labor markets with wages that adjust instantaneously. In this extreme scenario, describe what the SRAS curve looks like and why, using MOD-2.C.2 and MOD-2.E.1.

options.label: A
options.text: The SRAS would be horizontal — perfectly competitive markets drive wages to zero.

options.label: B
options.text: The SRAS would be upward-sloping — more competition means more elastic supply.

options.label: C
options.text: The SRAS would be vertical — with instantaneously adjusting wages (fully flexible), any price level rise is immediately matched by a proportional wage increase. Real wages are unchanged, profit margins are unchanged, and firms have no incentive to change output. Output stays at its natural (potential) level regardless of the price level — a vertical supply curve. This is identical to the LRAS: when wages are perfectly flexible in the short run, the "short run" AS becomes the same as the LRAS.

options.label: D
options.text: The SRAS would be downward-sloping — flexible wages reduce profit margins when prices rise.

options.label: E
options.text: The SRAS would be horizontal at the wage rate level — wages and prices equalize at all output levels.

explanation: MOD-2.E.1: MOD-2.C.2 states the SRAS slopes upward because of STICKY wages; if wages are instead perfectly flexible (instantaneous adjustment), the sticky-wage mechanism disappears entirely. Any PL rise → wages rise proportionally immediately → real wages unchanged → no profit-margin widening → no incentive to change output → output stays at potential. The SRAS becomes VERTICAL - identical to the LRAS; confirms: "In the long run all prices and wages are fully flexible" → vertical LRAS; perfect flexibility converts the SRAS into the LRAS graphically.
